newsitem.title: USA: Iraq has not rebuilt air defense - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iraq has not rebuilt air defense - U.S..

text.p: The White House said on Tuesday it had no indication Iraq had fully rebuilt its air defence system in southern Iraq but acknowledged there had been some activity at air defence sites despite U.S. threats.
In any case, spokesman Mike McCurry said, Iraq's air defence system posed no threat to U.S. and allied pilots flying missions over southern Iraq to enforce a no-fly zone.

The Washington Post quoted an unnamed "senior defence official" on Tuesday as saying in a recent interview that Iraq rebuilt a surface-to-air missile system in southern Iraq within two weeks of the United States launching 44 Cruise missiles against the system on Sept. 2 and 3.

The United States launched the attack in retaliation for Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's military push into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq in support of one Kurdish faction, the Kurdistan Democratic Party.

The Post said that since the attack the Iraqis have not used the surface-to-air missile radar or their Soviet-made SA-2 and SA-3 missiles in any threatening way but it quoted the official as saying it would take just "a flip of the switch" to turn on the targeting radar to create a military threat to U.S. and allied military planes.

McCurry, asked if the fixed air defence sites had been fully rebuilt, said Washington had no knowledge of that. He acknowledged there had been some "activity" at the sites but said there was no indication of any intent on Iraq's part to challenge the coalition aircraft patrolling the southern "no- fly" zone established after the 1991 Gulf War.
"They have not been rebuilt to the point where they are now being employed actively by Saddam Hussein to threaten international pilots enforcing the no-fly zone," he said.

He also said there was no evidence that Iraqi air defence systems were targeting U.S. and international aircraft in the no-fly zone, which he said would be considered a provocative act to which pilots would have a right to respond.
"We consider his air defence capacities degraded," McCurry told reporters travelling with President Bill Clinton.

McCurry also said Saddam seemed to be taking a cautious attitude toward air defence deployments. He said there was evidence Iraq was moving some of its mobile air defence sites, which were not targeted by the cruise missiles, but none of these movements threaten the no-fly zone pilots.

Other U.S. spokesmen said there was no evidence that either Iranian or Iraqi forces were involved in new Kurdish fighting in northern Iraq. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon was less definite, however, about Iraqi involvement.
"We do not have evidence that there is Iranian involvement," Bacon said. "And we do not have clear evidence of Iraqi involvement at this time either. We're watching it closely. That's all I can say."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said he understood the Kurdish faction backed by Iran had retaken much of the territory it lost to the Iraq-supported faction in September.
Burns said U.S. officials were trying to promote peace negotiations between the Kurdish factions but said he knew of no plan for a direct meeting between them and U.S. officials in Washington.
